II-36.explain: After birth, lung expansion and oxygen should drop pulmonary resistance; in PPHN it stays high, so blood takes the fetal shortcuts right-to-left.
II-36.hook: PPHN = the baby 'forgot' to switch off fetal circulation.

checks.q: In PPHN, what fails to happen after birth?
options: Pulmonary vascular resistance fails to fall
checks.why: PVR stays high; the open duct is a consequence, not the primary defect.

checks.q: Which direction is the shunt at the PDA and foramen ovale in PPHN?
checks.why: High pulmonary pressure pushes blood right-to-left, causing cyanosis.

II-36.explain: Anything that injures lungs or causes hypoxia/acidosis keeps pulmonary vessels constricted; some drugs and lung hypoplasia remodel vessels before birth.

checks.q: What is the commonest cause of PPHN?
checks.why: Meconium aspiration leads; sepsis, asphyxia and RDS are other causes.

checks.q: Which maternal drug in pregnancy is linked to PPHN?
checks.why: SSRIs (and NSAIDs, which close the duct early) are associated with PPHN.

II-36.explain: Blood that skips the lungs never meets the oxygen, so raising FiO2 does little; hypoxia then tightens vessels further.
II-36.hook: Vicious circle: hypoxia → constriction → more shunt → more hypoxia.

checks.q: Why does raising FiO2 barely help in PPHN?
checks.why: Right-to-left shunt bypasses ventilated alveoli, unlike parenchymal disease.

checks.q: Which two factors drive more pulmonary vasoconstriction in PPHN?
checks.why: Hypoxia + acidosis constrict pulmonary vessels, closing the vicious circle.

II-36.explain: A term baby who is bluer than the lungs explain, with swinging saturations, points to shunting; high pulmonary pressure gives a loud P2.
II-36.hook: Blue out of proportion + labile sats = think PPHN.

checks.q: Typical PPHN cyanosis is described as?
options: Out of proportion to lung disease
checks.why: Cyanosis exceeds the lung findings because of extrapulmonary shunting.

checks.q: Which heart sound is typical in PPHN?
checks.why: Raised pulmonary pressure gives a loud single S2, plus a TR murmur.

II-36.explain: The right hand is pre-ductal; legs are post-ductal. A gap shows ductal right-to-left shunt; echo proves it and excludes structural heart disease.

checks.q: Which pre-post-ductal saturation gap suggests PPHN?
checks.why: A gap over 3% (right hand higher) indicates ductal right-to-left shunting.

checks.q: Which test confirms the shunt and excludes cyanotic heart disease?
checks.why: Echo shows the shunt and rules out lesions such as TAPVD.

II-36.explain: Calm the baby and avoid triggers of vasoconstriction, dilate pulmonary vessels selectively with iNO, and keep systemic pressure above pulmonary.
II-36.hook: Calm, warm, iNO, pressors, then ECMO.

checks.q: Which is part of general PPHN care?
checks.why: Stimulation causes vasoconstriction; hyperoxia should be avoided too.

checks.q: At what oxygenation index is inhaled nitric oxide started?
checks.why: iNO 20 ppm is given if OI >20-25; it relaxes vessels via cGMP.

checks.q: What is used if PPHN is refractory to medical therapy?
checks.why: ECMO is the rescue after BP support (milrinone, adrenaline, vasopressin) fails.

II-37.explain: Babies can catch infections at three times: through the placenta, during passage through the birth canal, or after birth.
II-37.hook: Three routes: Before, During, After birth.

checks.q: Which is NOT a route of perinatal infection?
checks.why: Routes are transplacental, intrapartum and postnatal.

II-37.explain: Bloodborne agents cross the placenta; genital-tract and blood organisms infect at delivery; hospital lines and hands infect afterwards.
II-37.hook: Placenta = TORCH; canal = GBS/HSV; NICU = CoNS.

checks.q: Which is a transplacental perinatal infection?
checks.why: Parvovirus B19 crosses the placenta, like TORCH, VZV and Zika.

checks.q: Which infection is typically acquired intrapartum?
checks.why: GBS is acquired from the birth canal during delivery.

checks.q: Commonest NICU line-associated organism postnatally?
checks.why: CoNS from lines and hands are classic postnatal NICU pathogens.

II-37.explain: Early infection disrupts organ formation, causing malformations; late infection causes active disease. Infant immunity tolerates HBV, so chronicity is common.

checks.q: Infection in early pregnancy typically causes?
checks.why: Organogenesis is hit early; later infections cause active disease at birth.

checks.q: Roughly what proportion of infected infants become HBV carriers?
checks.why: Up to 90% of infants infected with HBV become chronic carriers.

II-37.explain: HSV targets brain, skin and liver. Conjunctivitis timing tracks the organism's incubation: chemical within a day, gonococcus fast, chlamydia slower.

checks.q: Which triad fits neonatal HSV?
checks.why: HSV causes seizures (encephalitis), vesicles and hepatitis.

checks.q: Gonococcal conjunctivitis typically appears at which age?
checks.why: Gonococcus 2-5 days; chlamydia 5-14 days; silver nitrate gives chemical conjunctivitis.

II-37.explain: Screening the mother lets you prevent transmission: treat or immunise the baby at birth or give intrapartum prophylaxis.
II-37.hook: Screen mum: HIV, HBV, syphilis, GBS.

checks.q: Which is part of routine antenatal infection screening?
checks.why: Antenatal screening covers HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis and GBS status.

II-37.explain: Each organism has a specific prophylaxis or drug; passive plus active immunisation blocks HBV, and HIV is avoided via ART and no breastfeeding.
II-37.hook: HBV baby: jab + HBIG within 12 h.

checks.q: Within what time should HBV vaccine + HBIG be given?
checks.why: Give within 12 hours (latest 24 h); breastfeeding is still allowed.

checks.q: What is the treatment for neonatal gonococcal infection?
checks.why: Gonococcus → ceftriaxone; chlamydia → azithromycin.

checks.q: Which feeding advice applies to HIV-positive mothers here?
checks.why: Per the notes: ART and no breastfeeding.

II-38.explain: TORCH groups congenital infections with overlapping features: growth restriction, eye and brain damage, rash and organomegaly.
II-38.hook: TORCH: Toxo, Other, Rubella, CMV, HSV.

checks.q: In TORCH, what does the 'C' stand for?
checks.why: C = cytomegalovirus; Other covers syphilis, VZV, parvovirus, Zika.

II-38.explain: Maternal infection crosses the placenta; damage is worst in the first trimester when organs are forming. CMV is the most frequent.

checks.q: Which is the commonest congenital TORCH infection?
checks.why: CMV is the commonest; risk of severe damage is highest in the 1st trimester.

II-38.explain: These organisms attack rapidly dividing fetal cells, so growth, brain and eyes suffer. Parvovirus destroys red cell precursors, causing hydrops.

checks.q: TORCH organisms damage the fetus by attacking?
checks.why: Attacking dividing cells causes IUGR, CNS and eye damage.

checks.q: Which congenital infection causes hydrops fetalis?
checks.why: Parvovirus B19 → fetal anaemia → hydrops; VZV → limb hypoplasia.

II-38.explain: Each agent has a signature: calcification pattern (CMV periventricular, toxo diffuse), the eye lesion, and for syphilis nose and bone signs.
II-38.hook: CMV circles the ventricles; toxo scatters everywhere.

checks.q: Which calcification pattern is typical of congenital CMV?
checks.why: CMV gives periventricular calcification; toxo gives diffuse calcification.

checks.q: Which triad suggests congenital rubella?
checks.why: Rubella: cataract, deafness, PDA; the second option is toxoplasmosis.

checks.q: Which sign is typical of congenital syphilis?
checks.why: Syphilis: snuffles, desquamating rash, saber shins.

II-38.explain: After 21 days, a positive CMV PCR could be postnatal infection, so testing must be early; most babies look normal, hence follow-up.

checks.q: Within how many days must CMV urine/saliva PCR be done?
checks.why: Within 21 days to prove congenital (not postnatal) infection.

checks.q: How is congenital toxoplasmosis diagnosed per the notes?
checks.why: Toxoplasmosis is diagnosed by antibody testing.

II-38.explain: Targeted antimicrobials for each agent; rubella has no cure, so prevention by vaccination is the strategy.

checks.q: Treatment of symptomatic congenital CMV?
checks.why: Symptomatic CMV: valganciclovir for 6 months.

checks.q: How is congenital rubella prevented?
checks.why: Rubella is prevented by MMR; syphilis is treated with penicillin G.

checks.q: HSV lesions present in labour: delivery method?
checks.why: Active lesions in labour → C-section; aciclovir from 36 weeks.

II-39.explain: Timing reflects source: early sepsis comes from the mother's genital tract, late sepsis from hospital or community exposure.
II-39.hook: 72 hours splits mother's bugs from the ward's bugs.

checks.q: What cut-off separates early- from late-onset neonatal sepsis?
checks.why: Early <72 h = vertical; late >72 h = nosocomial/community.

II-39.explain: Early organisms come from the birth canal; late ones from lines and the environment. Long membrane rupture and chorioamnionitis raise early risk.
II-39.hook: Early = GEL: GBS, E. coli, Listeria.

checks.q: Which organism is a classic early-onset sepsis cause?
checks.why: Early: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; Candida is late-onset.

checks.q: Commonest late-onset cause linked to central lines?
checks.why: CoNS colonise lines and dominate late-onset sepsis.

II-39.explain: Neonates have few neutrophils in reserve and low complement and antibodies, while lines breach skin barriers, so infection spreads fast.
II-39.hook: Empty neutrophil bank + open skin door.

checks.q: Why does neonatal sepsis spread rapidly?
checks.why: Small neutrophil reserve plus low complement/Ig allows rapid spread.

II-39.explain: Neonates rarely mount fever or focal signs; sepsis shows as non-specific changes in breathing, temperature, feeding and perfusion.
II-39.hook: Any 'off' baby is septic until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Which describes neonatal sepsis signs?
checks.why: Apnoea, temperature instability, grunting, poor feeding and mottling.

II-39.explain: Culture identifies the organism, serial CRP tracks inflammation, LP excludes meningitis. Maternal swabs flag GBS colonisation.

checks.q: Which is part of the neonatal sepsis work-up?
checks.why: Blood culture, serial CRP and lumbar puncture.

checks.q: Which sepsis agent is found by maternal vaginal screening?
checks.why: Official answer: GBS is identified by maternal vaginal screening.

II-39.explain: Intrapartum penicillin needs time to reach the baby; empirical antibiotics must be fast and cover GBS, Gram-negatives and Listeria.
II-39.hook: Penicillin ≥4 h before birth; antibiotics within 1 h.

checks.q: Intrapartum GBS penicillin must start how long before delivery?
checks.why: At least 4 hours; it does not prevent late-onset GBS.

checks.q: Empirical regimen for sepsis without meningitis?
checks.why: Ampicillin + gentamicin within 1 h; cefotaxime replaces gentamicin if meningitis.

checks.q: Previous baby had invasive GBS: what next pregnancy?
options: Screen and treat only if positive
checks.why: A prior invasive GBS baby means intrapartum prophylaxis every pregnancy.

II-40.explain: Preterm brains bleed (IVH) or suffer white matter ischaemia (PVL); term brains suffer global hypoxia, stroke, infection or trauma.
II-40.hook: Preterm: bleeds and white matter; term: HIE.

checks.q: Which CNS disorders typify preterm neonates?
checks.why: Preterm: IVH and PVL; term: HIE, stroke, infection, kernicterus, trauma.

II-40.explain: IVH strikes very preterm babies early; HIE is the leading cause of seizures. Instrumental delivery and traction cause trauma injuries.

checks.q: What is the commonest cause of neonatal seizures?
checks.why: HIE is the commonest seizure cause; IVH occurs <32 weeks within 72 h.

checks.q: Subgaleal haemorrhage typically follows which delivery?
checks.why: Vacuum extraction causes subgaleal bleeding; lateral traction causes Erb palsy.

II-40.explain: The germinal matrix is fragile and richly vascular, so it bleeds; periventricular white matter is a watershed area prone to ischaemia.
II-40.hook: PVL hits the leg fibres → spastic diplegia.

checks.q: Where does IVH originate?
checks.why: The fragile germinal matrix bleeds, risking hydrocephalus.

checks.q: PVL classically leads to?
checks.why: Watershed white matter ischaemia → PVL → spastic diplegia.

II-40.explain: Neonatal seizures lack tonic-clonic patterns. A boggy swelling crossing sutures with shock means bleeding under the galea.

checks.q: IVH sign related to head size?
checks.why: IVH: low tone, seizures, rapidly increasing head circumference.

checks.q: Scalp swelling crossing sutures with shock suggests?
checks.why: Subgaleal bleeds cross sutures and can cause shock; cephalohaematoma doesn't cross.

II-40.explain: Ultrasound through the fontanelle images bleeds; seizures first need reversible metabolic causes excluded before EEG.

checks.q: What does Papile grade IV IVH represent?
checks.why: Grade IV = periventricular haemorrhagic infarction on cranial ultrasound.

checks.q: Which tests come first in neonatal seizures?
checks.why: Check glucose and calcium first, then sodium, magnesium, infection; EEG.

II-40.explain: Phenobarbital is the first antiseizure drug in neonates. IVH is prevented by maturing vessels and keeping cerebral flow stable. Most plexus palsies recover.
II-40.hook: Pheno first; Erb heals 80% in 3 months.

checks.q: First-line drug for neonatal seizures?
checks.why: Phenobarbital is first line.

checks.q: Which helps prevent IVH?
checks.why: Antenatal steroids, magnesium, delayed cord clamping; avoid pressure/CO2 swings.

checks.q: Erb palsy: rate of spontaneous resolution within 3 months?
checks.why: About 80% resolve spontaneously within 3 months.

II-41.explain: Newborn skin and cord problems range from harmless rashes needing reassurance to infections needing urgent treatment.

checks.q: Which is NOT in the neonatal skin/umbilical topic?
checks.why: The topic covers benign rashes, vascular lesions, skin infections and umbilical problems.

II-41.explain: Benign rashes reflect immature skin and glands; infections come from staph, candida, HSV and cord colonisation.
II-41.hook: Erythema toxicum, milia, miliaria: all harmless.

checks.q: Which newborn skin finding is benign?
checks.why: Erythema toxicum is benign; the others are infective.

checks.q: Which is an infective neonatal skin condition?
checks.why: SSSS (and bullous impetigo, candida, HSV, omphalitis) are infective.

II-41.explain: Staph toxin splits desmoglein-1 in superficial epidermis only, so mucosa is spared. Cord infection can track along the umbilical vein.

checks.q: What does SSSS exfoliative toxin cleave?
checks.why: Desmoglein-1 is skin-only, so mucosa is spared (unlike pemphigus vulgaris dsg-3).

checks.q: Omphalitis can spread via the umbilical vein to cause?
checks.why: Omphalitis → umbilical vein → sepsis and portal vein thrombosis.

II-41.explain: Look at what is in the lesion and where umbilical discharge comes from: the urachus links bladder, the vitelline duct links gut.

checks.q: Erythema toxicum pustules are full of?
checks.why: Sterile pustules packed with eosinophils.

checks.q: Natural course of strawberry haemangioma?
checks.why: Infantile haemangioma proliferates, then involutes.

checks.q: Urine leaking from the navel indicates?
checks.why: Urine = patent urachus; faeces = vitelline duct.

II-41.explain: Neutrophils are needed to separate the cord; failure of adhesion (CD18) delays it. A single umbilical artery is a marker for other anomalies.

checks.q: Delayed cord separation with neutrophilia suggests?
checks.why: LAD (CD18 defect): neutrophils can't leave vessels; normal separation 5-15 days.

checks.q: A single umbilical artery raises suspicion of?
checks.why: Single umbilical artery is associated with congenital/chromosomal anomalies.

II-41.explain: Treat only what threatens function or health: propranolol for dangerous haemangiomas, cautery for granulomas, antibiotics/antivirals for infections.

checks.q: Indicated drug for haemangioma threatening eye or airway?
checks.why: Propranolol if eye, airway or ulceration involved.

checks.q: Umbilical hernia usually resolves by what age?
checks.why: Monitor; most resolve by age 5. Granuloma → silver nitrate.

checks.q: Treatment of SSSS?
checks.why: SSSS → IV flucloxacillin; omphalitis IV antibiotics; HSV aciclovir.

II-42.explain: NEC is bowel death in preterm infants once feeding begins; meconium ileus is a thick-meconium obstruction that strongly points to CF.

checks.q: NEC typically occurs in preterms after what?
checks.why: Ischaemic-inflammatory necrosis begins after feeds start.

checks.q: Meconium ileus is strongly associated with?
checks.why: Meconium ileus is a CF presentation (~15% of CF).

II-42.explain: Immaturity is the key driver; formula and dysbiosis add risk, whereas breast milk's factors protect the gut.

checks.q: Biggest risk factor for NEC?
checks.why: Prematurity is the biggest risk factor; breast milk is protective.

II-42.explain: Weak barrier, wrong bacteria and poor blood flow let bacteria invade the bowel wall and produce gas within it.
II-42.hook: Gas in the wall = bacteria in the wall.

checks.q: What does bacterial invasion of the bowel wall in NEC produce?
checks.why: Bacteria invade the wall and produce intramural gas: pneumatosis.

II-42.explain: NEC shows gut failure (distension, intolerance, blood) and systemic sepsis; meconium ileus shows low obstruction with no stool passed.
II-42.hook: NEC triad: distension, intolerance, bloody stool.

checks.q: Which triad matches the official NEC symptoms?
checks.why: Official answer: abdominal distension, nutritional intolerance, bloody stool.

checks.q: Which feature fits meconium ileus?
checks.why: Distension, bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium.

II-42.explain: X-ray reveals gas where it shouldn't be; a cross-table lateral picks up free air when the baby can't be moved. Meconium ileus shows a small unused colon.
II-42.hook: Rigler = both bowel wall sides seen = perforation.

checks.q: What does Rigler sign indicate in NEC?
checks.why: Rigler sign (both sides of bowel wall visible) means free air = perforation.

checks.q: Immobile baby with NEC: how to detect perforation?
checks.why: Official answer: horizontal X-ray from side position with baby lying on back.

checks.q: Which X-ray finding suggests meconium ileus?
checks.why: Soap-bubble and microcolon; sweat test later.

II-42.explain: Rest the bowel, decompress, support nutrition and cover gut flora; operate if perforated. Gastrografin's osmotic action loosens meconium.

checks.q: Core medical NEC treatment includes?
checks.why: Bowel rest (NPO), NG decompression, IV fluids, TPN, IV antibiotics.

checks.q: Which is an indication for surgery in NEC?
checks.why: Perforation, peritonitis or deterioration despite medical therapy.

checks.q: First-line treatment for uncomplicated meconium ileus?
checks.why: Gastrografin enema; surgery if it fails.

II-43.explain: CDH is mostly a left posterolateral defect; OA leaves a blind upper pouch, usually with a fistula from the trachea to the lower oesophagus.

checks.q: Typical location of a Bochdalek hernia?
checks.why: Bochdalek CDH is usually left-sided posterolateral; Morgagni is anterior.

checks.q: Most common OA type has?
checks.why: Proximal blind pouch with distal TEF in 85%.

II-43.explain: Gut in the chest squeezes the developing lung; OA is part of a mesodermal defect spectrum, so other anomalies coexist.
II-43.hook: VACTERL: vertebral, anal, cardiac, TE, renal, limb.

checks.q: OA/TEF is associated with which anomaly cluster?
checks.why: OA/TEF is part of VACTERL (mesodermal defects).

II-43.explain: In CDH, lung underdevelopment and pulmonary hypertension decide outcome. In OA, fluid can't be swallowed, causing polyhydramnios and drooling.

checks.q: What determines survival in CDH?
checks.why: Pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension determine survival.

checks.q: Which pregnancy finding accompanies OA?
checks.why: Fetus can't swallow amniotic fluid → polyhydramnios.

II-43.explain: Bowel in the chest empties the abdomen and shifts the heart; OA babies can't clear saliva. An H-type fistula without atresia causes feeding cough.
II-43.hook: CDH: scaphoid belly, heart on the right.

checks.q: Which abdominal sign suggests CDH?
checks.why: Viscera in chest leave a scaphoid abdomen; heart sounds shift right.

checks.q: Classic early sign of OA?
checks.why: Excess drooling and choking at first feed.

checks.q: Cough since birth, always with feeds, suggests?
checks.why: H-type TEF: no atresia, but feeds pass into the airway.

II-43.explain: A firm tube stops and coils in the upper pouch. Gas in the stomach means air enters via a distal fistula; no gas means pure atresia.
II-43.hook: Coiled tube + gas = OA with distal TEF.

checks.q: Gastric gas with a coiled NG tube indicates?
checks.why: Gas in stomach requires a distal fistula; pure OA gives gasless abdomen.

checks.q: Pure OA without fistula gives what on X-ray?
checks.why: Gasless abdomen; also screen VACTERL and do echo.

II-43.explain: Bag-mask would inflate gut in the chest, so intubate. Stabilise lungs and pulmonary pressure before repair. In OA, suction the pouch first.

checks.q: Which airway step is avoided in CDH?
checks.why: Bag-mask inflates herniated bowel; intubate and place NG tube.

checks.q: CDH surgery timing?
checks.why: CDH is a physiological, not surgical, emergency.

checks.q: Before OA/TEF surgery, which tube is placed?
checks.why: A Replogle tube suctions the upper pouch; look for VACTERL.

II-44.explain: This group covers blockages along the gut and defects of the abdominal wall where bowel lies outside.

checks.q: Which is an abdominal wall defect?
checks.why: Gastroschisis and omphalocele are wall defects; the others are obstructions.

II-44.explain: Duodenal atresia is an early recanalisation failure (Down link); jejunoileal atresia follows a later vascular accident. Omphalocele links to syndromes.

checks.q: Which chromosomal abnormality links to duodenal atresia?
checks.why: Official answer: trisomy 21; jejunoileal atresia is vascular.

checks.q: Gastroschisis is associated with?
checks.why: Gastroschisis: young mothers; omphalocele: BWS, trisomies 13/18.

II-44.explain: Bile enters below the ampulla, so blockage beyond it gives bilious vomiting; the fetus can't absorb swallowed fluid, causing polyhydramnios.

checks.q: Obstruction below the ampulla causes which vomiting?
checks.why: Below the ampulla, bile enters: bilious vomiting from first feed.

II-44.explain: High blockage leaves a flat belly; low blockage gives many dilated loops. Omphalocele is midline in a sac; gastroschisis is bare, to the right.

checks.q: Duodenal atresia abdominal appearance?
checks.why: High obstruction: bilious vomiting with flat abdomen.

checks.q: Gastroschisis lies where relative to the cord?
checks.why: Right of cord, no membrane; omphalocele is midline with a sac.

checks.q: Which defect has more associated major malformations?
checks.why: Omphalocele has cardiac, GU and neural tube anomalies.

II-44.explain: Air fills the stomach and proximal duodenum with nothing beyond: two bubbles. Malrotation with volvulus must be excluded.

checks.q: Radiological sign of duodenal atresia?
checks.why: Official answer: double bubble; exclude malrotation.

II-44.explain: Decompress and rehydrate, then bypass the atresia. Exposed bowel needs protection from fluid and heat loss. High anal atresia needs a stoma first.

checks.q: Definitive surgery for duodenal atresia?
checks.why: Decompress, fluids, then duodenoduodenostomy.

checks.q: If primary gastroschisis closure fails, what is used?
checks.why: Wrap in sterile saline dressings; primary closure else staged silo.

checks.q: How is defecation ensured in high anal atresia?
checks.why: Official answer: colostomy, then PSARP; low lesions get anoplasty.

II-45.explain: BPD is defined by ongoing respiratory support at 36 weeks corrected; ROP is disordered growth of retinal vessels in preterm eyes.
II-45.hook: BPD = still on O2 at 36 weeks.

checks.q: BPD is defined as oxygen or support at what PMA?
checks.why: BPD = O2 or respiratory support at 36 weeks PMA.

checks.q: ROP is a disorder of?
checks.why: Abnormal retinal vessel growth in preterm babies.

II-45.explain: Immature lungs and eyes are damaged by too much oxygen, ventilation pressure and inflammation.
II-45.hook: Oxygen helps but harms the preterm.

checks.q: Besides prematurity, which is a key cause of BPD?
checks.why: Oxygen toxicity, ventilator trauma and infection on top of prematurity.

II-45.explain: Injury halts alveolar and vessel growth, leaving fewer, simpler alveoli. In ROP, high oxygen then relative hypoxia triggers VEGF-driven abnormal vessels.
II-45.hook: ROP: oxygen → hypoxia → VEGF → new vessels.

checks.q: BPD lungs show which alveolar change?
checks.why: Arrested growth leaves simplified alveoli, plus pulmonary hypertension.

checks.q: Which mediator drives neovascularisation in ROP?
checks.why: Hypoxic retina releases VEGF → neovascularisation.

II-45.explain: BPD babies need oxygen for weeks and show scarring on X-ray. Preterm follow-up watches growth, development, hearing and vision.

checks.q: BPD chest X-ray shows?
checks.why: Ground-glass opacities from scarring, with prolonged oxygen need.

checks.q: PVL in a preterm leads to which outcome?
checks.why: PVL → spastic diplegia, so neurodevelopment is followed.

II-45.explain: Correct for prematurity when judging growth and milestones until ~2 years, but vaccinate by real age. Screen small/early babies for ROP.
II-45.hook: Corrected for milestones; chronological for jabs.

checks.q: Which age is used for preterm vaccination?
checks.why: Vaccines use chronological age; growth/development use corrected age.

checks.q: ROP screening criterion?
checks.why: Screen <31 weeks or <1501 g; BPD with rising O2 needs echo.

II-45.explain: Preterms lack iron and vitamin D stores and are vulnerable to RSV. Prevent BPD by maturing lungs; treat ROP by stopping neovascular drive.

checks.q: Which is used for RSV prevention in preterms?
checks.why: Nirsevimab or palivizumab; supplement iron and vitamin D.

checks.q: Which helps prevent BPD?
checks.why: Maternal glucocorticoids, surfactant, caffeine; optimise oxygen and nutrition.

checks.q: Treatment for ROP?
checks.why: Laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF.

II-46.explain: Hodgkin is defined by Reed-Sternberg cells and peaks in adolescents; childhood NHL is almost always aggressive high grade.

checks.q: Which cell defines Hodgkin lymphoma?
checks.why: Reed-Sternberg cells; childhood NHL is high grade.

II-46.explain: Burkitt is driven by MYC translocation; nodular sclerosis dominates Hodgkin subtypes.

checks.q: Which translocation is typical of Burkitt lymphoma?
checks.why: t(8;14) moves MYC next to the IgH locus.

checks.q: Commonest Hodgkin subtype?
checks.why: Nodular sclerosis is commonest (70%).

II-46.explain: Hodgkin's RS cells recruit inflammatory cells and spread node to node; cytokines cause B symptoms. Burkitt cells divide fast and lyse en masse.
II-46.hook: TLS: high K, PO4, urate; low Ca.

checks.q: Hodgkin lymphoma spreads how?
checks.why: Contiguous spread; cytokines cause B symptoms.

checks.q: Which TLS finding is low?
checks.why: Phosphate binds calcium, so calcium falls; K, phosphate, urate rise.

II-46.explain: Lymphoma nodes are painless and rubbery; B symptoms show systemic disease. Burkitt favours the abdomen; lymphoblastic the mediastinum.

checks.q: Which weight loss counts as a B symptom?
checks.why: B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10%.

checks.q: Lymphoblastic lymphoma typically presents with?
checks.why: Lymphoblastic → anterior mediastinal mass; Burkitt → abdominal mass.

checks.q: Which node size is suspicious?
checks.why: Suspicious: >2 cm, hard, supraclavicular, persistent.

II-46.explain: Whole-node excision preserves architecture for diagnosis; steroids can melt lymphoma and spoil the biopsy.

checks.q: Reed-Sternberg cells are positive for?
checks.why: RS cells are CD15+, CD30+; staging with CXR and PET-CT.

checks.q: Which drug must be avoided before lymph node biopsy?
checks.why: Steroids can shrink lymphoma and make biopsy non-diagnostic.

II-46.explain: Hodgkin is highly curable; therapy intensity adapts to response. Rasburicase breaks down urate but produces H2O2, dangerous in G6PD deficiency.
II-46.hook: Mediastinal mass: don't lie them flat.

checks.q: Cure rate of childhood Hodgkin lymphoma?
checks.why: Response-adapted chemotherapy cures >90%.

checks.q: Rasburicase is contraindicated in which condition?
checks.why: Rasburicase generates H2O2 → haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

checks.q: With a mediastinal mass, what should be avoided?
checks.why: Avoid GA and lying flat: risk of airway compression.

II-47.explain: Leukaemia is the commonest childhood cancer, and most is ALL, peaking in preschool years.

checks.q: Peak age of childhood ALL?
checks.why: ALL ~80% of childhood leukaemia, peak 2-5 years.

II-47.explain: Down syndrome increases leukaemia risk markedly.

checks.q: Which syndrome is a key risk factor for leukaemia?
checks.why: Down syndrome is a classic risk factor.

II-47.explain: Blasts crowd out normal marrow, so all cell lines fall; they also infiltrate bone and organs, and hide in the CNS beyond chemo's reach.

checks.q: Why is the CNS important in leukaemia?
checks.why: CNS is a sanctuary; hence intrathecal methotrexate.

II-47.explain: Marrow failure gives pallor, bleeding and infection; infiltration gives bone pain, organomegaly and nodes. T-ALL arises in thymus.

checks.q: Which leukaemia type has a mediastinal mass?
checks.why: T-ALL arises from thymic T cells → mediastinal mass.

II-47.explain: Marrow examination confirms leukaemia; flow and genetics classify and stratify. MRD after treatment is the strongest prognostic marker.

checks.q: What is the test for acute leukaemia?
checks.why: Official answer: bone marrow examination, plus flow cytometry and genetics.

checks.q: Strongest prognostic factor in ALL?
checks.why: MRD is strongest; good: age 1-10, WBC <50, hyperdiploidy/ETV6-RUNX1.

II-47.explain: Multi-phase chemo over ~2 years with CNS-directed therapy cures most. Neutropenic fever is an emergency. Donor immune cells fight leukaemia after SCT.

checks.q: Which drug is given intrathecally in ALL?
checks.why: Intrathecal methotrexate treats the CNS sanctuary; cure ~90%.

checks.q: Febrile neutropenia: antibiotics within?
checks.why: IV antibiotics within 1 hour; co-trimoxazole prevents Pneumocystis.

checks.q: What is graft versus leukaemia?
checks.why: Official definition: donor cells' immune attack on leukaemic cells.

II-48.explain: Platelets plug small vessels, so their failure causes skin and mucosal bleeding; joint bleeds suggest a clotting factor problem.

checks.q: Platelet disorders typically bleed into?
checks.why: Skin and mucosa; joint bleeds suggest coagulation factor deficiency.

II-48.explain: Low count arises from destruction or underproduction; normal count with bleeding means dysfunction.
II-48.hook: Normal count, still bleeding → function defect.

checks.q: Which is a destructive cause of thrombocytopenia?
checks.why: ITP destroys platelets; aplasia and leukaemia reduce production.

checks.q: Which has normal count but platelet dysfunction?
checks.why: Glanzmann, Bernard-Soulier, vWD, aspirin: normal count, poor function.

II-48.explain: ITP antibodies coat platelets for splenic removal. Without ADAMTS13, large vWF multimers form clots. Glanzmann lacks aggregation; Bernard-Soulier adhesion.
II-48.hook: Glanzmann = Gather fails; Bernard-Soulier = Binding fails.

checks.q: ITP antibodies target which platelet glycoprotein?
checks.why: IgG against GPIIb/IIIa; platelets cleared by splenic macrophages.

checks.q: TTP results from deficiency of?
checks.why: ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves uncleaved vWF → microthrombi.

II-48.explain: Platelet bleeding shows as petechiae and epistaxis; brain bleeding is the dreaded outcome. ITP: well child after a virus, no big organs.
II-48.hook: ITP: well child, post-viral, isolated purpura.

checks.q: Most feared complication of thrombocytopenia?
checks.why: Intracranial haemorrhage is the feared complication.

checks.q: Purpura 3 weeks after a viral illness, well child?
checks.why: Official answer: ITP; no organomegaly fits.

II-48.explain: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion with only platelets low, and the marrow compensates. Other abnormalities demand marrow exam to exclude leukaemia.
II-48.hook: Other line low or HSM → marrow.

checks.q: ITP blood film typically shows?
checks.why: Large young platelets; marrow has increased megakaryocytes.

checks.q: When is bone marrow needed in suspected ITP?
checks.why: Other line low, HSM or bone pain → marrow to exclude leukaemia.

II-48.explain: Most childhood ITP remits, so skin-only bleeding is watched; treat bleeding with steroids/IVIG. Reactive thrombocytosis needs no treatment.

checks.q: Childhood ITP with cutaneous bleeding only?
checks.why: Observe: 75-80% resolve in 6 months; mucosal bleeding → steroids.

checks.q: Treatment for chronic ITP (>12 months)?
checks.why: TPO agonists romiplostim/eltrombopag; IVIG for significant bleeding.

checks.q: Management of reactive thrombocytosis?
checks.why: Reactive thrombocytosis needs no treatment and no aspirin; TTP → plasma exchange.

II-49.explain: DIC consumes clotting factors and platelets; HUS and TTP are thrombotic microangiopathies that shred red cells.
II-49.hook: HUS triad: MAHA, low platelets, AKI.

checks.q: Which is NOT part of the HUS triad?
checks.why: Triad: MAHA, thrombocytopenia, AKI; clotting times are normal.

checks.q: TTP involves deficiency of which enzyme?
checks.why: ADAMTS13, the vWF metalloprotease.

II-49.explain: Severe systemic insults trigger DIC. Shiga toxin E. coli causes typical HUS; complement dysregulation causes atypical HUS.

checks.q: Which is a cause of DIC?
checks.why: Sepsis, shock, trauma, malignancy.

checks.q: Which E. coli serotype causes typical HUS?
checks.why: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 after bloody diarrhoea.

checks.q: Atypical HUS is due to?
checks.why: Alternative complement pathway dysregulation.

II-49.explain: Tissue factor triggers widespread clotting that uses up factors, so patients clot and bleed. Shiga toxin injures glomerular endothelium via Gb3.
II-49.hook: Gb3 = toxin's door on the glomerulus.

checks.q: Which initiates DIC?
checks.why: Tissue factor → microthrombi + consumption + fibrinolysis.

checks.q: Shiga toxin binds which receptor?
checks.why: Gb3 on glomerular endothelium → microthrombi, RBC fragmentation, AKI.

II-49.explain: DIC paradoxically causes both clots and bleeding. HUS follows bloody diarrhoea with pallor, bruising and kidney failure.
II-49.hook: DIC = clot and bleed at once.

checks.q: DIC clinically shows?
checks.why: Consumption causes bleeding while microthrombi cause thrombosis.

checks.q: HUS typically follows?
checks.why: Anaemia, low platelets, AKI after bloody diarrhoea.

II-49.explain: DIC uses up factors and fibrinogen (long clotting times, low fibrinogen) and breaks clot (high D-dimer); HUS spares the clotting cascade.

checks.q: Fibrinogen level in DIC?
checks.why: Low fibrinogen, low platelets, prolonged PT/APTT, high D-dimer.

checks.q: Which distinguishes HUS from DIC?
checks.why: Clotting is normal in HUS but prolonged in DIC.

II-49.explain: Treat DIC's trigger and replace products only if bleeding. Typical HUS is supportive; antibiotics may release more toxin. Block complement in atypical HUS.

checks.q: Cornerstone of DIC management?
checks.why: Treat the cause; platelets, FFP, cryo only if bleeding.

checks.q: What should be avoided in typical HUS?
checks.why: Avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs; supportive care/dialysis.

checks.q: Treatment of atypical HUS?
checks.why: Eculizumab (anti-C5); TTP → plasma exchange, steroids, rituximab.

II-50.explain: A block in haem synthesis causes the substrates before it to pile up; which substrate accumulates determines the symptoms.

checks.q: In porphyria, what accumulates?
checks.why: Precursors before the enzyme block accumulate.

II-50.explain: AIP is dominant PBG deaminase deficiency; PCT (UROD) is commonest overall; EPP (ferrochelatase) commonest in children. Enzyme inducers raise ALA synthase.

checks.q: Which enzyme is deficient in AIP?
checks.why: AIP: autosomal dominant PBG deaminase (HMBS) deficiency.

checks.q: Most common porphyria overall?
checks.why: PCT (UROD deficiency) is the most common porphyria.

checks.q: Commonest porphyria in children?
checks.why: EPP (ferrochelatase deficiency); P-450 inducers trigger attacks.

II-50.explain: Early precursors (ALA, PBG) are neurotoxic, giving acute attacks; late porphyrins absorb light, causing skin damage.

checks.q: Which precursors are neurotoxic?
checks.why: Early precursors ALA and PBG cause acute neurovisceral attacks.

checks.q: Late porphyrins cause what?
checks.why: Late porphyrins cause photosensitivity.

II-50.explain: AIP: neurovisceral attacks with dark urine and no skin signs. Hyponatraemia is from SIADH. PCT gives blistering on sun-exposed skin.

checks.q: Which feature is absent in AIP?
checks.why: AIP has no photosensitivity (early precursors only).

checks.q: Hyponatraemia in an AIP attack is due to?
checks.why: SIADH causes hyponatraemia in attacks.

checks.q: PCT presents with?
checks.why: Blistering cutaneous photosensitivity and hyperpigmentation.

II-50.explain: During an attack, PBG floods the urine, making it the quick screening test.

checks.q: Screening test in an acute porphyria attack?
checks.why: Urinary PBG, with raised ALA.

II-50.explain: Haem and glucose switch off ALA synthase, cutting precursor production. PCT is treated by lowering iron or mobilising porphyrins.

checks.q: Acute attack treatment?
checks.why: Haemin and glucose inhibit ALA synthesis; barbiturates are contraindicated.

checks.q: Which treats PCT?
checks.why: PCT: low-dose hydroxychloroquine or phlebotomy.
